title: Christian Nationalism: An 8-Week Study
subtitle: A pastoral, even-handed five-session study that names what Christian nationalism is and is not, indicts every tribe, and keeps the cross over the flag.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of a phrase that has been thrown like a rock in two directions and want to know what it actually names. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell, defining Christian nationalism without slandering the man whose grandfather landed at Normandy, and confronting the fusion of nation and faith without sneering at ordinary patriotic believers. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters one party and indicts the other. It catches the right and the left both. It asks the conservative whether he has married his country to God and refused to let anyone file for divorce, and it asks the progressive whether he fears religion in public only when it is the wrong religion. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He came up out of atheism into a faith already fused with the flag, he still has flags on his own platform he has not moved, and he writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What It Is and What It Is Not
sessions.aim: To define Christian nationalism precisely as the fusion of nation and faith into one loyalty that cannot be questioned, distinct from ordinary patriotism.
sessions.summary: A man left Bell's office certain his pastor had insulted his grandfather, who landed at Normandy. He had not. The phrase Christian nationalism has been ruined in both directions, used as a slur against patriotic faith by some and as a catchall for people I disagree with who pray by others. Between those two distortions the real thing has nearly disappeared. Bell makes the strongest case for the man who fears the phrase before answering it. Loving your country is not a sin. Scripture tells exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon. But the scholars who coined the careful term, Whitehead and Perry, defined it as a cultural framework that fuses American civic identity with Christian identity, holds the nation has a covenant with God, and believes the kingdom of Christ can be advanced by capturing the state. The key word is fuses. Patriotism loves a country and can repent. Nationalism has made the nation the thing that judges, so it cannot. The covenant many assume is ancient was legislated in living memory, one nation under God added in 1954, in God we trust in 1956.

keyScripture.why: Jesus tells Pilate his kingdom is not of this world, which should have ended Christian nationalism before it was born.

discussion.q: When you first heard the phrase Christian nationalism, what did you assume it meant, and where did that assumption come from?
discussion.behind: Surface the two distortions in the room before defining anything. Some will hear a slur against patriots, some a catchall for the other side. The point is not to settle it yet but to show that everyone arrived with a loaded definition. Land it on humility, not consensus.

discussion.q: Bell says patriotism loves a country and nationalism worships it, and the test is what happens when your country and your Christ command different things. Can you name a real moment that test would expose?
discussion.behind: Push past the abstract. You want a concrete fork, an actual conflict between a national loyalty and an obedience to Christ. If they cannot name one, that itself is the finding, because the nationalist has arranged his theology so the conflict can never arise.

discussion.q: The phrase one nation under God entered the Pledge in 1954 and in God we trust became the motto in 1956. What does it do to the idea of an ancient covenant to learn its dates?
discussion.behind: The aim is to loosen the assumption of an eternal Christian founding without mocking it. A covenant you can date to an act of Congress is a national mood that learned to talk like one. Let them sit in the discomfort rather than rescuing them from it.

discussion.q: Whitehead and Perry found the strongest Christian nationalism often among people who do not attend church much. Why should that stop a believer cold?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. It means the thing is less a deep faith than an identity, a way of marking the boundary of the nation with religious language. It can flourish in a heart with very little of Christ in it. Listen for the recognition that this is not really about Jesus.

discussion.q: Bell says he is not standing outside this but writing toward himself, that he has wanted his country to be the kingdom. Where do you feel that pull in yourself?
discussion.behind: Move the table from diagnosis to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone. You want each person, including you the leader, inside the indictment, because you cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue.

objections.objection: This whole study is just a way for the left to sneer at conservative Christians who love their country and their flag.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true before you answer. Carelessly throwing the phrase at faithful people who feed the hungry and bury the poor is its own sin, and Bell says he will not defend it. Then make the distinction gently. The study is not against loving your country. It is against the fusion that cannot repent. You can honor the grandfather at Normandy and still ask whether his grandson crossed a line he never saw.

objections.objection: Warnings about religion in public are selective. People only fear faith in the public square when it is the wrong faith, and a faith driven out of public life is just another establishment wearing the mask of neutrality.
objections.response: Grant it fully, because Newbigin saw exactly this. There is no neutral public square. The question is never whether faith shapes public life but which faith and how. Affirm the person, then point out that this is a critique of false neutrality, not a defense of fusion. The answer to a hidden establishment is not to enthrone our own. It is honest, humble public faith that can still be corrected.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one thing you love about your country that you would never want to lose?
sessions.practice: This week, notice once when you feel a stronger reaction to an insult against your country than to an insult against Christ. Do not fix it. Just notice the temperature, and write down what it told you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have loved our country, and that love is not the sin. The sin is when we let it grow too large to be corrected. Show us the line at our feet that we keep stepping over without noticing. Keep the cross above the flag in us this week, and give us the humility to be told the truth about what we have made ultimate. In the name of the King whose kingdom is not of this world, amen.
reflection: Where did I first learn to fuse my faith and my country, and did anyone ever teach it to me on purpose, or was it just in the air I breathed?
What would it cost me to admit my country could be wrong about a thing I care about, and why does that cost feel so high?
If Christ and my country commanded different things tomorrow, do I actually know which one I would obey, or have I arranged my life so the question never comes up?
sessions.teaching: Start where the man in the office started. He left certain his pastor had insulted his grandfather, the one who landed at Normandy, because he heard the phrase Christian nationalism as an accusation against everyone who ever stood for a flag with a hand over the heart. He was wrong about what was said. He was right to be careful. So we are going to be careful too. We are going to say what this thing is not before we say what it is, at length and in good faith, because the phrase has been ruined in two directions at once. To one side it is a slur against ordinary patriotic faith. To the other it is a lazy catchall that means little more than people I disagree with who pray. Between those two distortions the real thing has nearly vanished, and we cannot resist a thing we cannot name. I want to make the strongest case for the man who fears the phrase, because his case has weight. Loving your country is not a sin. Scripture told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon, to build houses and plant gardens and pray for the city that was not even theirs. Gratitude for a country and its soldiers and its harvests honors the gifts of God. And the people who throw the phrase around have often never set foot in his church or watched his people feed the hungry and bury the poor. He is right about all of that, and the carelessness of his accusers is its own sin. Now hear the turn. Everything he just described is patriotism, and patriotism is not what the phrase names. The careful scholars who coined the term, Whitehead and Perry, defined it as a cultural framework that fuses American civic identity with a particular Christian identity, holds the nation has a covenant with God, and believes the kingdom can be advanced by capturing the state. The word that does the work is fuses. Patriotism loves a country. This marries the country to God and then refuses to let anyone file for divorce. Niebuhr drew the line plainly. Love of country is a high devotion that becomes demonic the moment it claims the unconditioned loyalty belonging to God alone. So the test is not whether you sing the anthem or honor the dead. The test is what happens when your country and your Christ command different things. The patriot grieves and obeys Christ. The nationalist has quietly arranged his theology so the conflict can never arise. And the covenant many assume is ancient is not ancient at all. One nation under God entered the Pledge in 1954. In God we trust became the motto in 1956. A covenant you can date to an act of Congress is a national mood that learned to talk like one. One more finding should stop us cold. The strongest expressions of this fusion often show up among people who barely attend church, which means it was never really about Jesus. It was about the nation, dressed in his name. I am not standing outside this. The first faith handed to me out of atheism was already fused with the flag, and I did not question it for years. So we will all stand inside it together.

scriptureStudy.note: Jesus answers Pilate, the man holding Rome's power in that room, with a sentence that should have ended this whole argument. He does not deny he is a king. He denies the kind.
The Greek 'ek tou kosmou' means out of, sourced from. He is not saying his kingdom has no bearing on this world. He is saying it does not originate here and does not run on this world's fuel.
The proof he offers is strange and decisive. If his kingdom were of this world, his servants would be fighting. A kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by definition.
Hold this beside John 18 to keep the balance. Exiles are told to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray for it. Love of a place is commanded, even a place that is not your own.
When Israel wants a king to be like the nations, God names it as rejecting him from being king. The desire to be like the nations is never merely political.
The kingdom God sets up is not handed to another people and breaks every other kingdom in pieces. It is given, not seized, which is the opposite of a movement that plans to capture the state.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the historiography the essay only gestures at. Mark Noll in America's God argues that the colonists did not arrive with a unified Christian nation in mind and that the founders ranged from devout Calvinists to skeptical deists, which complicates any clean story of a Christian founding lost and waiting to be reclaimed. Set that against the nineteenth-century construction of providentialism, the habit of reading God's favor directly off national events, which Noll treats as a genuine theological error rather than mere bad history. The deeper move is to see Christian nationalism as a rival soteriology, a full account of sin and salvation in which the nation is the vehicle of redemption, its founding a covenant, its decline a fall, its restoration a work faithful citizens must accomplish. Once you see that structure you can ask whether Jesus is actually at the center of it or merely its mascot. For the seminary-trained group, work the distinction between Augustine's two cities and the two-kingdoms tradition that runs through Luther and into modern Reformed thought, and ask where each protects the church from fusion and where each can be abused to excuse passivity. Then test Whitehead and Perry's methodology honestly. Their spectrum is built on survey items, and a careful group should ask what those items capture and what they miss, where the sociology is strong and where a believer should hold it loosely. The aim is not to weaponize the data but to learn its limits.
sessions.caseStudy: A retired Army veteran in your group has said little all evening. When you reach the question about dates, he finally speaks. His father flew bombing runs over Germany. He says that when you put the words 1954 and 1956 next to the Pledge and the motto, it feels like you are calling his father's faith a fad, something Congress invented, and he is not sure he can keep coming if that is where this is headed. He is not angry. He is wounded, and the room goes quiet because everyone respects him. Here is the test for the leader and the group. Can you honor him fully, grant that his father's faith was real and his service was real, and still let the dates stand as dates. The point was never that his father was a fraud. The point is that an arrangement can feel eternal and still have a birthday, and learning the birthday does not insult the people who lived inside it. Sit with him. Do not rush to rescue the room from the discomfort.

memoryVerse.text: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.

devotional.title: The Man in the Office
devotional.body: Begin where the essay begins, with a man who heard an insult that was never spoken. He loved his grandfather. He loved his country. He had built an identity where to question the one felt like betraying the other, so a careful phrase landed on him like a rock. Before you decide what you think about Christian nationalism, sit with how easy it is to hear an attack where only a question was asked. We do this constantly. Someone names a fault in a thing we love and we feel the heat rise before we have understood the words. That heat is information. It tells you where your loves are tangled, where you have fused something to your own worth so that an honest question feels like an assault. The exiles in Babylon had every reason to despise the city that held them, and God told them to seek its welfare and pray for it. That is a love that can survive the truth about the city. Ask God today to give you a love for your country sturdy enough to hear it questioned without flinching, and humble enough to learn something from the person asking.
devotional.prayer: Father, show me where I have fused my worth to a thing that can be questioned. Give me a love steady enough to hear hard words without hearing an enemy. Make me slow to take offense and quick to understand.

devotional.title: Two Distortions
devotional.body: The phrase has been ruined in two directions, and both directions are sins of the tongue. One side uses it as a slur, a way to dismiss faithful people without listening to them. The other side hears it as a slur no matter how carefully it is meant. The proverb says the one who states his case first seems right until another comes and examines him. Most of our fights about this are people stating their case first and loudly and never letting the other come to examine it. We arrive with a loaded definition and call it discernment. Today, resist the reflex to define the person across from you by the worst version of his position. The careful term names something real and dangerous, but it has been thrown so often without care that the careful meaning has nearly drowned. Recovering it requires the patience to say what a thing is not before you say what it is. That patience is a form of love. It refuses the cheap win of a caricature. Ask whether you have been more interested in being right about this than in being truthful, and whether those two things have quietly come apart in you.
devotional.prayer: Lord, guard my tongue from the cheap slur and my ears from the false offense. Teach me the patience to understand before I answer. Let me want the truth more than the win.

devotional.title: The Word That Does the Work
devotional.body: Fuses. That is the word. Patriotism loves a country and can repent of it. Christian nationalism fuses the country to God so that the two can no longer be told apart, and a thing you cannot tell apart from God you can no longer correct. Jesus said no one can serve two masters, that you will love the one and hate the other, or hold to one and despise the other. We hear that text about money and skip past how completely it applies to nations. The problem is rarely that we consciously choose the country over Christ. The problem is the fusion, the quiet welding that makes us think they always want the same thing, so the choice never has to be made out loud. That is more dangerous than open idolatry, because open idolatry at least knows it has two masters. Fusion forgets there were ever two. Ask God today to show you one place where you have assumed your country and your Christ want the same thing, and to give you the courage to test the assumption instead of resting in it.
devotional.prayer: Master, I cannot serve two and you have told me so plainly. Show me where I have fused what should stay separate. Pull the seam apart so I can see which one I am actually serving.

devotional.title: A Covenant With a Birthday
devotional.body: One nation under God entered the Pledge in 1954. In God we trust became the motto in 1956. Many believers carry these phrases as proof of an ancient covenant, and they are younger than people still in our pews. This is not an attack on the phrases. It is an invitation to honesty about where our sense of a Christian founding actually comes from. Deuteronomy warns the people not to say in their heart, my power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth. The national version of that sin says, our founding and the favor of God have gotten us this greatness, and it reads providence directly off our own history as though we could be sure God was on our side. Scripture is far more careful than we are about such certainties. God used Assyria as a rod and then broke the rod. A nation can be an instrument in his hand and still stand under his judgment. Today, hold your country's story more loosely. Thank God for genuine gifts in it without claiming you know the verdict of heaven on its founding. That humility is not disloyalty. It is the beginning of telling the truth.
devotional.prayer: Lord, keep me from reading my own favor into your providence. Let me thank you for real gifts without claiming a covenant you never made. Teach me a humbler patriotism.

devotional.title: The Line at Your Feet
devotional.body: Niebuhr said love of country becomes demonic the moment it claims the unconditioned loyalty that belongs to God alone, and most of us cross that line without ever seeing it. Paul warns the one who thinks he stands to take heed lest he fall. The danger is not for the obvious zealot who waves the fusion like a banner. The danger is for the ordinary believer who is sure he would never confuse the flag and the cross, and who has therefore stopped watching the line at his feet. The test is simple and merciless. What happens in you when your country is wrong. Not in theory, where everyone admits it could be. In the moment, when a specific failure is named and your throat tightens to defend rather than to grieve. That tightening is the line being crossed. End this week by asking God to make you a person whose love of country can still hear the country corrected, who grieves its sins instead of denying them, who keeps the cross above the flag not as a slogan but as the actual order of his loves. You cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue.
devotional.prayer: Father, I think I stand, so guard me from the fall I cannot see. Show me the line at my feet. Make my love for my country small enough to be corrected and my worship of you large enough to fill its proper place. Amen.

sessions.title: Loving Versus Worshiping Your Country
sessions.aim: To draw the line between love, which can be corrected, and worship, which cannot, and to test which one we give our country.
sessions.summary: Bell's oldest son asked, after a parade, why we put our hands over our hearts. The honest answer is that we make the same gesture in two settings, before the flag and when we pray, and a child notices the rhyme an adult has stopped hearing. Love and worship are not opposites. Worship is what love becomes when it stops admitting any limit. Bell defends the love before warning against the worship, because the warning is dishonest without the defense. A Christian may love his country truly. Scripture told exiles to love Babylon. But the line is plain. Love can be corrected and worship cannot, because correction assumes a standard above the thing and worship has put the thing where no standard reaches it. The test is not how you feel at the parade. It is what you do when your country is wrong. Niebuhr called nationalism the point where patriotism becomes demonic, claiming the unconditioned loyalty that belongs to God alone. Augustine called sin disordered love, the lesser good loved as though it were the greatest. The problem was never the size of the love. It was the place the love was put.

keyScripture.why: When Israel demands a king to be like the nations, God says they have rejected him from being king, naming the desire as a transfer of trust.

discussion.q: Bell says the same hand goes over the heart in front of the flag and in prayer. What do you make of the two gestures being identical?
discussion.behind: Let the image do the work. You are not trying to prove the gesture is idolatry. You are helping them feel the rhyme a child hears and an adult has tuned out, so the rest of the session has somewhere to land.

discussion.q: The test, Bell says, is not how you feel at the parade but what you do when your country is wrong. Walk through it. What does the lover do, and what does the worshiper do?
discussion.behind: You want the contrast crisp. The lover says my country and grieves and resists. The worshiper says my country and defends it, because the alternative is that his god has failed. Listen for anyone who realizes they cannot remember the last time they let their country be wrong.

discussion.q: Augustine says sin is disordered love, the lesser good loved above the greater. Where, honestly, does love of country sit in your own order of loves?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the session. The drunk does not love wine too much in a simple sense. He loves it out of order. Help people see the question is not how much they love their country but where that love sits relative to the kingdom, the stranger, and Christ.

discussion.q: In 1 Samuel, wanting a king to be like the nations was a transfer of trust away from the God they could not see. Where do you see that same trade today, and does it run left or right?
discussion.behind: Keep it even-handed here on purpose. The desire to be like the nations shows up in a conservative longing for a strong Christian country and in a progressive trust in the state to deliver salvation. Both are the same trade. Do not let the room make it a one-party sin.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he has grown hot at an insult to the flag and cool at an insult to the cross, and that the temperature gauge does not lie. What is your gauge telling you?
discussion.behind: Close the diagnostic loop with self-implication. The thing you defend most fiercely is the thing you actually worship, whatever your mouth confesses on Sunday. Go first as the leader if the room is slow.

objections.objection: Every warning against nationalism cuts one direction. Nobody scolds the rootless cosmopolitan who feels nothing for any place. The suspicion of patriotism is really just contempt for ordinary people and their loyalties.
objections.response: Bell agrees the contempt is real and common. A man who loves nowhere is not holier than a man who loves somewhere, and rootlessness is not a virtue. Affirm that fully. Then clarify the target. This is not an argument for the cold heart. It is an argument for the difference between a warm heart and an enthroned one. We are not asking anyone to love their country less. We are asking where the love sits.

objections.objection: You say wanting your country to be great is really rejecting God as king. That just baptizes passivity and lets injustice run because Christians are too holy to want anything for their nation.
objections.response: This is the progressive-leaning version, and it deserves the same care. Wanting good for your country is not the sin. Israel was told to seek the welfare of Babylon. The trade God named was trust, not action, the moving of ultimate hope from the God they could not see to the strength they could point to. You can labor hard for justice in your country and still refuse to make the country your god. The two are not in tension.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When was the last time you felt your throat tighten with love for a place or a people?
sessions.practice: This week, find one specific way your country has been wrong about something, name it out loud to one person, and notice whether your love survives the correction. If it does, that is the love God permits. If it cannot, that is the worship he forbids.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you alone sit at the top where no standard reaches you, and we keep trying to put other things there. We have loved good gifts out of order. We have defended what we should have grieved. Reorder our loves. Let us love our country with a love that can still tell it the truth, and let our worship belong to you alone, who were killed by an empire and rose anyway. Amen.
reflection: What do I defend most fiercely, and what does that reveal about what I actually worship?
Can I name a single time I have let my country be wrong out loud, and if not, what does that silence tell me?
Where in my life is a good love sitting in the wrong order, above something or someone it should serve rather than rule?
sessions.teaching: Open with the child's question, because a child hears what an adult has tuned out. Bell's oldest son asked, after a parade, why we put our hands over our hearts. The easy answer is respect and the dead. The honest answer is that we make the same gesture in two rooms, in front of the flag and when we pray, and the rhyme between them is the whole subject tonight. The question underneath the child's question is the oldest one a believer faces. What may I love, and how much, before love becomes worship. Notice that love and worship are not opposites. Worship is what love becomes when it stops admitting any limit. And a country is one of the easiest things in the world to love past its limit, because it asks for that love openly, with music and graves and the names of the fallen, and to withhold it feels like betraying the dead. So defend the love first, because the warning is dishonest without the defense. A Christian may love his country truly. The same Scripture that exiled Israel told them to love Babylon, to seek its welfare, to plant gardens in it. The throat that tightens at a military funeral is not sinning. That is love, and love is good, and the people who sneer at it have usually never loved a place enough to be embarrassed by their own tears. Now draw the line, and draw it plainly. Love can be corrected. Worship cannot. You can love your wife and still tell her she is wrong, still refuse to follow her into evil, and the love survives the correction and even deepens through it. But the thing you worship cannot be corrected, because correction assumes a standard above the thing, and worship has put the thing at the top where no standard reaches. So the test of whether you love your country or worship it is not how you feel at the parade. It is what you do when your country is wrong. The lover says my country and grieves and resists. The worshiper says my country and defends it, because the alternative would mean his god has failed. Niebuhr called this the point where patriotism becomes demonic, claiming the unconditioned loyalty that belongs to God alone. He did not choose the word demonic for effect. He meant that a good thing loved past its limit does not stay good and merely shrink. It becomes a power that demands sacrifice and silences conscience. Augustine gave us the cleanest name a millennium and a half earlier. Sin is disordered love, the lesser good loved as though it were the greatest. The drunk does not love wine too much in a simple sense. He loves it out of order, above his health and his family and God. The nationalist does not love his country too much. He loves it out of order, above the kingdom and the stranger and the Christ who said the stranger bears God's image. The problem was never the size of the love. It was the place the love was put. Then carry the hardest text. When Israel demanded a king to be like the nations, God told Samuel they had not rejected Samuel, they had rejected God from being king over them. The desire to be like the nations was a transfer of trust, away from the God they could not see and toward the strength they could point to. And here I have to step into the indictment, because the line runs through me. I have grown hot at an insult to the flag and cool at an insult to the cross, and the temperature gauge does not lie. The thing you defend most fiercely is the thing you actually worship, whatever your mouth confesses on Sunday.

scriptureStudy.note: God tells Samuel to obey the voice of the people, which is a mercy and a judgment at once. He gives them what they ask, and the gift becomes the discipline.

They have not rejected you, they have rejected me from being king over them. The sin is named as a transfer of kingship, not a policy preference. The throne changed hands in the heart before it changed in the nation.
The stated motive is to be like all the nations. The longing to look like the powers around them is the engine, and it runs underneath both right and left to this day.
God spells out the cost. The king they want will take their sons, their daughters, their fields, their best. The thing you enthrone to save you will eventually conscript you.
The people refuse to listen and insist on a king to fight their battles. Worship of strength always promises to fight your battles, and it always sends your children to do it.

Read the first commandment behind all of it. No other gods before me is not about statues. It is about the place a thing occupies, and a country can occupy that place while everyone insists they still worship God.

sessions.goingDeeper: Work the Augustinian frame to its root. In On Christian Doctrine Augustine distinguishes things to be enjoyed, frui, from things to be used, uti, and locates sin precisely in enjoying what was meant to be used and using what was meant to be enjoyed. A nation belongs to the order of penultimate goods, real and to be loved, but to be referred upward to the God who alone is to be enjoyed for his own sake. Christian nationalism is, in this grammar, the enjoyment of a penultimate thing as though it were ultimate, which is the structural definition of idolatry rather than a matter of degree. Set this beside Niebuhr's account in The Irony of American History, where the danger is not the wicked nation but the virtuous one, the nation whose genuine goodness tempts it to imagine its power is innocent. A seminary group should hold the tension between Augustine, who locates the disorder in the individual soul's loves, and Niebuhr, who locates it in the collective self-deception of nations and warns that groups are far more capable of sustained self-justification than persons. Then test 1 Samuel 8 against the wider canon. The monarchy is both a judgment on Israel's unbelief and the line through which David and ultimately Christ come. That tension matters, because it forbids the lazy reading that all national structure is simply faithless. God works through the king he warned against. The deeper question is not whether nations may exist but where trust finally rests.
sessions.caseStudy: A progressive member of your group, a social worker, has been nodding along all evening, comfortable that this study is aimed at the conservatives she argues with at family dinners. Then you reach the question about whether the trade runs left or right. She says, almost offhand, that of course the government should be the one to fix poverty and injustice, that this is just what loving your neighbor looks like at scale. The room waits. Here is the even-handed moment the session is built for. Her instinct is good and her concern for the poor is real, and you should say so plainly. But press the gentle question. Where exactly does her hope rest. If the state is the thing she trusts to deliver salvation, to finally make the world right, she has made the same trade Israel made when they wanted a king to be like the nations, only her king wears a different color. The desire to be like the nations shows up as a conservative longing for a strong Christian country and as a progressive trust in the state to save. Both are the same transfer of trust. Do not let the room aim this at one side only.

memoryVerse.text: And the Lord said to Samuel, Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.

devotional.title: Two Rooms, One Gesture
devotional.body: We put a hand over the heart in front of the flag, and we fold the same hands when we pray. A child notices the rhyme an adult has stopped hearing. The point of the rhyme is not that honoring a country is wrong. It is that the body learns devotion through repetition, and the same posture in two rooms can quietly teach the heart that the two rooms hold the same kind of thing. Jesus said to love the Lord your God with all your heart and soul and mind, the whole of you, nothing held back. That total claim leaves room for lesser loves underneath it but not beside it. The trouble begins when a lesser love starts standing at the same height as the highest one, sharing its gestures, asking for its devotion. Today, pay attention to your own postures. Notice what you stand for, what makes you put a hand to your chest, what stirs the same feeling in you that worship is meant to stir. Then ask whether those feelings are pointed at the right room. The body is honest. It will show you where your devotions are aimed if you watch it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you ask for all of me, and I have given pieces to lesser things and called it loyalty. Show me what shares your gestures in my heart. Teach me which room is which.

devotional.title: Seek the Welfare of the City
devotional.body: Before any warning lands, hear the permission. God told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon, to build and plant and pray for the city that held them captive. This is not grudging tolerance. It is a command to love a place that was not even their own. If God told exiles to love Babylon, how much more may you love the country that raised you and fed you and buried your father. The Christian who fears that this study will shame his love of country should rest here. The love is permitted. The love is even commanded. Rootlessness is not a virtue, and the cosmopolitan who feels nothing for any place is not holier than the man whose throat tightens at a familiar hymn. Today, do not be afraid of your love for your home and your people. Let it be warm. Thank God for the specific place he set you, its rivers and its roads and its dead. The whole point of drawing a line between love and worship is to set love free to be itself, sturdy and unashamed, without the weight of a devotion it was never meant to carry.
devotional.prayer: Father, thank you for the place you set me, its gifts and its people and its graves. Let me love it freely and well. Keep that love in its proper room, warm and unashamed and never enthroned.

devotional.title: Disordered Love
devotional.body: Augustine taught that sin is disordered love, the lesser good loved as though it were the greatest. Paul says the human race exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped the creature rather than the Creator. Notice that idolatry in Paul is not the love of evil things. It is the love of created things put in the place of the Creator, good gifts asked to be God. The drunk does not love wine too much in a simple sense. He loves it out of order. The nationalist does not love his country too much. He loves it out of order, above the kingdom and the stranger. This should be a relief and a warning at once. A relief, because it means you do not have to stop loving your country to be faithful. A warning, because the disorder is subtle, a matter of position rather than presence, and you can carry it for years without noticing. Today, take an honest inventory of your loves and ask not how much you love each thing but where each one sits. The question is the order, not the size. What have you placed above what.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you are the one to be loved for your own sake, and everything else loved through you. Reorder my loves. Pull down what I have raised too high and lift what I have let fall.

devotional.title: A King Like the Nations
devotional.body: The people would not listen. They wanted a king to be like the nations, a king to go before them and fight their battles. God read the desire correctly. It was not a policy preference, it was a transfer of trust, away from the God they could not see and toward the strength they could point to. He gave them the king, and the king taxed them and took their sons and led them into the ruin they had been warned about. Here is the part we miss. This same trade runs in every direction. The conservative who longs for a strong Christian nation to fight his battles and the progressive who trusts the state to deliver justice are making one trade in two costumes. Both want a visible strength to do what they no longer trust the invisible God to do. Today, find the place where you have asked a human power to be your king, to fight the battle you are afraid God will not fight. Name it honestly. The desire to be like the nations is never merely political. It is always, underneath, a quiet handing back of the throne.
devotional.prayer: King of heaven, I have wanted a king I could see, a strength I could point to, and called it wisdom. Forgive the trade. Be my king again, the one I cannot see and dare not replace.

devotional.title: The Temperature Gauge
devotional.body: Bell confesses he has grown hot at an insult to the flag and cool at an insult to the cross, and that the gauge does not lie. The risen Christ tells the church at Ephesus that he holds this against them, that they have abandoned the love they had at first. They were busy and orthodox and tireless, and their first love had cooled, and Christ called it a thing to repent of. Notice he did not measure their faith by their activity but by the temperature of their love. So measure yours the same way. What raises your heat fastest. What insult lands hardest. The thing you defend most fiercely is the thing you actually worship, whatever your mouth confesses on Sunday. This is not a comfortable test, and it is not meant to be. End the week by letting it land. If your country can be mocked and you feel nothing, but a slight against your nation sets your blood moving, the gauge has told you the truth about the order of your loves. The mercy is that Christ names a cooled love not to condemn but to call it home. Repent, he says, and do the things you did at first.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, my gauge has told the truth and the truth does not flatter me. I have run hot for lesser things and cool toward you. Return me to my first love. Set the heat where it belongs. Amen.

sessions.title: Flags in the Sanctuary
sessions.aim: To examine how sacred space teaches, and why a national symbol placed beside the Word fuses two faiths whether or not anyone chose it.
sessions.summary: Two flags stand on the platform of the church where Bell learned to preach. He did not put them there, and neither did the pastors before him. They simply appeared in the middle of the last century, without a vote, and now to move them would feel like aggression while placing them would have felt like nothing. That asymmetry is the whole subject. We defend to the point of fury an arrangement we never chose to make. Bell makes the honest case for the flag first. It can be gratitude, an honor to those who served and did not come home, a recognition that the church lives in a real country. He grants that removal can be a sneer rather than a confession, performed pride rather than worship. Then he answers with a question about geography. Not the lobby, where we might thank God for a free country, but the platform, beside the pulpit, inside the jealous space the architecture reserves for Word and table and baptism. Placement is a sermon. Bellah showed civil religion is a real religion with sacred objects. Carry a sacred object from one faith into the holy space of another and you do not get nothing. You get fusion. Bell confesses he has not moved his own flags, because he knows what it would cost.

keyScripture.why: The glory of the Lord fills the temple so the priests cannot stand, showing the sanctuary as jealous space that tolerates no rival glory.

discussion.q: Bell notes we will fight to keep an arrangement we never chose to install. Why does a thing we never decided have more power over us than the things we did?
discussion.behind: Open on the asymmetry, not on flags specifically. The point is that inherited arrangements shape us beneath the level of choice. Help them see the flag is an example of a larger pattern in their own lives before it becomes a fight about cloth.

discussion.q: Bell asks where the flag stands, not whether it exists. Lobby or platform. Why does the geography change the meaning?
discussion.behind: Keep them on placement, not presence. A symbol beside the cross will eventually be read as the cross's equal. The eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech. You are after the recognition that location preaches.

discussion.q: Bellah said civil religion is a real religion with its own sacred objects and holy days. If that is true, what happens when a sacred object from one faith enters the holy space of another?
discussion.behind: You want the word fusion. The worshiper stops feeling the seam between the two faiths and experiences patriotism and Christianity as one undivided devotion, which is the precise definition of the thing. Tie it back to session one.

discussion.q: Bell says removing a flag can be a sneer as easily as keeping it can be idolatry, that a bare platform can serve pride. How do you tell the difference?
discussion.behind: This protects the even-handedness. The object is not the disease. The disease is in what the object is permitted to mean. Do not let the group conclude that stripping the platform automatically makes them holy. Pride wears both arrangements.

discussion.q: Bell admits the flags on his own platform have outlasted his objections, that he is the priest who has grown used to the second altar, not the prophet clearing the temple. Where are you the priest who has grown used to something?
discussion.behind: Self-implication again. The honest confession is that most of us let symbols stand because keeping them is easier than explaining them. Invite people to name their own unexamined second altar, not necessarily a flag.

objections.objection: Taking the flag off the platform is just the church being ashamed of its country and siding with the cultured people who look down on patriotic believers.
objections.response: Bell says this is sometimes exactly what removal means and exactly how it is meant, and he has seen it done as a sneer. Grant that honestly. The question is not settled by moving the cloth, because pride can strip a platform as easily as idolatry can drape one. The real work is on what the symbol is allowed to mean, not on scoring the country. Lead with honoring the dead and the freedom to gather, then ask the harder question about jealous space.

objections.objection: This is overthinking a piece of fabric. It is decoration. Reading idolatry into a flag stand is exactly the kind of elite suspicion that alienates ordinary people in the pew.
objections.response: Take the worry seriously, because contempt for ordinary believers is real. But Bell's point is not that the cloth is magic. It is that arrangement teaches beneath words, and a child raised beside two equal symbols absorbs the equality before he can name it. Bell says his own children have. This is not elite suspicion. It is a working pastor watching what his sanctuary teaches his sons whether he means it to or not.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Think of the room where you first learned to worship. What stood at the front, and what did the arrangement teach you?
sessions.practice: This week, walk through your own church or your own home and read the room like a sermon. What stands in the place of honor, and what is it quietly teaching the children who grow up looking at it? Just observe. Bring what you notice back next time.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of glory, you filled the temple until the priests could not stand, and you share your holy place with no rival. We have grown used to second altars and called them only cloth. Give us eyes to read the rooms we worship in. Where we have let a lesser glory stand beside the cross, give us the courage to pay the cost of moving it, and the honesty to admit when we have not. Amen.
reflection: What stands in the place of honor in the spaces where I worship, and what has it been teaching me without my consent?
Where am I the priest who has grown used to a second altar rather than the one willing to pay the cost of moving it?
What am I unwilling to examine because examining it would cost me something with the people around me?
sessions.teaching: There are two flags on the platform of the church where Bell learned to preach, and the strange thing is that almost nobody chose them. He did not put them there. Neither did the pastor before him or the one before that. They appeared sometime in the middle of the last century, without a vote, and they have guarded the Word ever since with an authority no business meeting ever granted. That is the asymmetry that is the whole subject. To move them now would feel like aggression. To have placed them would have felt like nothing. We will fight to keep an arrangement we never once chose to make, and a thing you would fight to keep but would never have thought to install has more power over you than the things you actually decided. Make the honest case for the flag first, because the people who make it are not fools. The flag in the sanctuary can be simple gratitude for the country that protects the freedom to gather. It can honor the members who served and did not come home, and removing it can wound the families of the dead for the sake of an abstraction. The church does not live in heaven yet but in a particular country under particular laws, and pretending otherwise is its own dishonesty. Every one of those points has weight. Go further and state the strongest version. Removing the flag is not neutral either. It can be a statement of its own, a signal that the church is ashamed of its country, that it has joined the cultured despisers who look down on ordinary patriotic believers. And that is sometimes exactly what removal means. Bell has seen the flag taken down as a sneer, not a confession, by people more eager to perform their sophistication than to worship. So the question is not settled by moving the cloth. A bare platform can serve pride as easily as a draped one can serve idolatry. The object is not the disease. The disease is in what the object is permitted to mean. Now answer it with a question about geography. Where does the flag stand. Not the lobby, where we might thank God for a free country. The platform. Beside the pulpit. Inside the space the architecture reserves for the Word and the table and the waters of baptism. The placement is a sermon, and it preaches every week whether anyone notices, because the eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech. A symbol that stands beside the cross will eventually be read as the cross's equal, and a child raised in that room absorbs the equality long before he could put words to it. Bell says his own children have. Bellah taught us to see civil religion as a real religion with its own sacred objects and holy days. Carry a sacred object from one faith into the holy space of another and you do not get nothing. You get fusion, a worshiper who can no longer feel the seam between the two faiths. And here is the confession underneath the essay. The flags on Bell's own platform have outlasted his objections to them. He is not the prophet clearing the temple. He is the priest who has grown used to the second altar and tells himself it is only cloth, because keeping it is easier than explaining it. The law lands on him first. So we will read our own rooms tonight, not to feel superior, but to ask what they have been teaching us without our consent.

scriptureStudy.note: When the priests came out of the holy place, the cloud filled the house so they could not stand to minister. The glory itself crowded them out. The sanctuary is the place where one presence dwells and fills.
The reason given is plain. The glory of the Lord filled the house. Not shared, not flanked, filled. The space was built for a single glory, and a single glory took it.
The second commandment forbids carved images and calls God jealous. The Hebrew 'qanna' is not petty envy but the rightful, exclusive claim of a covenant Lord over his own house.

King Ahaz moves the Lord's altar aside to set his own new altar in the prime place near the temple. He did not remove the true altar. He just gave the better spot to a rival. Placement was the whole sin.

Ezekiel sees an image of jealousy set up at the gate of the inner court and hears it called a great abomination that drives God far from his sanctuary. A symbol in the wrong space does real spiritual work.
You are God's temple and his Spirit dwells in you. Carry the principle from the building to the body. The question of what stands in the jealous space is now asked of your own heart.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up Bellah's 1967 essay on its own terms rather than as a slogan. Bellah argued that American civil religion was not simply a corruption but a genuine and partly noble phenomenon, capable of summoning the nation to judgment as Lincoln did at Gettysburg and in the Second Inaugural. The advanced question is therefore sharper than condemnation. If civil religion can humble a nation as well as flatter it, what determines which it does, and can a sacred object placed in a sanctuary ever serve the humbling function, or does the location itself collapse the critical distance civil religion needs to judge the nation. Bring in the theology of sacred space. The Old Testament's insistence on a jealous sanctuary is not arbitrary ritual law but a sustained pedagogy about the exclusivity of covenant worship, and the prophets read syncretism in the temple, the altars of other gods beside the Lord's, as the precise mechanism by which the house was lost. A seminary group should weigh the iconoclast and iconodule traditions here, since the essay's worry is not that images are evil but that arrangement teaches, which is closer to the iconodule conviction that material things form us than to a flat Reformed iconoclasm. Then face the hardest honest counterpoint. Cathedrals have long held the tombs and banners of the nation's dead, and Christendom routinely mingled throne and altar. Was that always fusion, or are there forms of honoring the dead that do not enthrone the nation. The leader should let that question stay open.
sessions.caseStudy: A long-tenured deacon, theologically conservative and deeply pro-life, surprises the room. He says he has been convicted that the two flags beside his church's pulpit are teaching his grandchildren something he never intended, and he wants to propose moving them to the fellowship hall. A younger member, also conservative, pushes back hard. He says this is exactly the kind of capitulation the culture wants, that the moment the church starts apologizing for the flag it has surrendered to the people who hate it, and that the deacon is letting the left set the agenda inside his own sanctuary. Both men love the same Lord and vote the same way. Here is the work. The younger man is right that removal can be a sneer and that the disease is in the meaning, not the cloth. The deacon is right that placement preaches and that a second glory in the jealous space teaches the children before they can name it. Do not resolve it for them. Let them feel that two faithful conservatives can read the same platform differently, and that the question is not which side wins but what the arrangement is allowed to mean.

memoryVerse.text: And the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the Lord filled the house of the Lord.

devotional.title: The Arrangement Nobody Chose
devotional.body: The flags appeared without a vote, and now to move them would feel like aggression while placing them would have felt like nothing. That asymmetry is worth a week of attention, because it is not really about flags. It is about how much of your life runs on arrangements you never chose and would now fight to keep. Jeremiah calls the people to stand at the crossroads and look and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it. Standing at the crossroads means stopping long enough to examine the path you are already on, the inherited one, the one that feels like the weather. Most of what forms us was handed to us before we could weigh it, the placement of symbols, the assumptions in the air, the loyalties we absorbed from a room. None of that is automatically wrong. But none of it is automatically right either, and the things we never decided have more power over us than the things we did, precisely because we never examined them. Today, find one inherited arrangement in your life of faith and simply look at it. Not to tear it down. To see it. To ask whether you would choose it now.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have inherited more than I have chosen, and I defend what I never examined. Help me stand at the crossroads and look. Give me the courage to see what I have only ever absorbed.

devotional.title: Where, Not Whether
devotional.body: Bell does not ask whether the flag exists. He asks where it stands. The lobby is one thing. The platform, beside the pulpit, inside the space reserved for Word and table and baptism, is another. When the temple was finished, the glory of the Lord filled the house so the priests could not stand to minister. The sanctuary is the place where one glory dwells, and it was built to be that way. The geography is the whole question because location preaches. A thing placed beside the cross will be read as the cross's equal, no matter what anyone says about it from the pulpit. The eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech. This is not only about church buildings. Your home has a place of honor too, a wall, a shelf, a screen that holds your attention at the center. Today, walk through the spaces you live in and read them as sermons. What occupies the place of honor. What has the central spot, the platform, the jealous space of your attention and your home. Whatever stands there is teaching you and the children who watch you, and the lesson is sinking in below the level of words.
devotional.prayer: God of glory, you fill your house and share it with no rival. Show me what I have placed in the center of my spaces and my attention. Let one glory have the platform of my life.

devotional.title: The Second Altar
devotional.body: King Ahaz did not tear down the Lord's altar. He simply moved it aside and put his own new altar in the better spot, the prominent place by the temple. That is how it usually happens. Not a dramatic rejection of God but a quiet reassignment of the prime real estate, the true altar still present but nudged from the center to make room for a rival that flatters more and asks less. Bellah called civil religion a real religion with its own sacred objects. When one of those objects takes the central spot, you have not removed God. You have given his place to something else and kept him on as a tenant. The danger of the second altar is exactly that it does not feel like apostasy. Everything looks intact. The Lord's altar is still there, just not where it was. Today, ask the uncomfortable question. Is there a second altar in your worship, a thing that has crept into the central place while God's altar quietly moved to the side. It need not be a flag. It can be a cause, a comfort, a fear. Look for what has the better spot.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have moved your altar to the side without meaning to and let a rival take the center. Forgive the quiet reassignment. Restore your place. Put you back where you belong in me.

devotional.title: Jealous Space
devotional.body: The second commandment calls God jealous, and we flinch at the word because we hear human pettiness in it. But the jealousy of God is the rightful, exclusive claim of a covenant Lord over what is his. A husband who feels nothing when his wife gives herself to another does not love her more, he loves her less. God's jealousy is the measure of how completely he has bound himself to his people and means to have them undivided. The sanctuary was built jealous on purpose, tolerating no rival glory, because the God who dwells there will not share the central place with the altars of the nations. This is not insecurity. It is love that refuses to be one option among several. Today, let the jealousy of God be a comfort rather than a threat. He wants the whole of you, the platform of your heart, not a wing of it shared with a dozen lesser glories. That total claim is the safest place you will ever stand, because the God who refuses to share you is the God who will never let you go. Ask him to clear the rivals from the jealous space and to be, for you, the single glory that fills the house.
devotional.prayer: Jealous God, you will not share me and I am glad of it. Clear the rivals from the center of me. Be the one glory that fills my house, undivided, unrivaled, alone.

devotional.title: The Priest Who Grew Used to It
devotional.body: Bell ends with a confession, not a verdict. The flags on his own platform have outlasted his objections. He is not the prophet clearing the temple. He is the priest who has grown used to the second altar and tells himself it is only cloth, because keeping it is easier than explaining it. The risen Christ says to the church at Laodicea that they think they are rich and need nothing, and do not know that they are poor and blind and naked. The most dangerous spiritual condition is not open rebellion. It is the comfortable blindness of the one who has grown used to things, who no longer sees the arrangement because he stopped looking long ago. Examining what we have grown used to costs something, usually a conflict with the people around us who have also grown used to it, and so we let it stand. End the week honestly. Where are you the priest who has grown used to a second altar rather than the one willing to pay the cost of moving it. The first step is not to move anything. It is to stop pretending you do not see it. Ask Christ for eyes that are willing to be opened, even though seeing will cost you the ease of not having seen.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, I have grown comfortable and called it peace, blind and called it settled. Open my eyes to the altars I have stopped seeing. Give me the honesty to look and the courage to pay what looking costs. Amen.

sessions.title: Whose Kingdom? Jesus and Political Power
sessions.aim: To settle from the wilderness, Pilate's hall, and the cross that the kingdom of God does not advance by seizing the means the world uses to win.
sessions.summary: Before Jesus preached or healed, he was taken to a high place and shown every kingdom of the world by one who actually had them to give. The price was a single act of worship aimed in the wrong direction. Jesus refused, and the refusal is the founding decision of his ministry. He would not take the kingdoms of the world on the terms by which they are taken. We reopen this every election as though he never settled it. Bell gives the strongest objection a full hearing. The prophets confronted kings, John the Baptist lost his head, Wilberforce ended a slave trade, Bonhoeffer joined a plot against Hitler. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people power crushes. Bell grants the whole of it. The error he warns against is not engagement but the belief that engagement means seizing the throne, that Christ needs to govern through Caesar because he cannot govern otherwise. The difference between Wilberforce and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup. To Pilate, Jesus said his kingdom is not of this world, and the proof he offered was the absence of fighting. On the cross he took the throne by the one means no empire understands. He did not seize power. He absorbed it.

keyScripture.why: The tempter offers Jesus every kingdom for one act of worship, and his refusal is the founding decision against advancing the kingdom by the world's means.

discussion.q: In the wilderness the kingdoms were really on the table, and the price was one act of misdirected worship. Why does it matter that the offer was real and not hollow?
discussion.behind: If the temptation was fake, it teaches nothing. Bell insists the kingdoms were available. The point is that real power is genuinely on offer to the church, and the modest-seeming price is always a redirected worship that says power saves. Set this up as the pattern the whole session returns to.

discussion.q: Bell says the difference between Wilberforce and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup. How do you tell faithful engagement from trying to seize the throne?
discussion.behind: This is the crucial distinction that keeps the study from sounding like withdrawal. Wilberforce pressed a particular evil with the tools at hand and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. He did not try to make Britain the kingdom of God. Listen for the line between pressing a cause and installing a kingdom.

discussion.q: To Pilate, Jesus offered the absence of fighting as proof his kingdom is not of this world. What does that do to the idea that the kingdom advances by winning?
discussion.behind: A kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by definition. The kingdom of God is recognizable by its refusal to take up the sword every earthly kingdom requires. Help them feel how disqualifying that is for any conquest theology.

discussion.q: The Palm Sunday crowd wanted a king to throw out Rome by force, and by week's end they wanted his blood because he would not be that king. Where do we still want the king who conquers instead of the one who dies?
discussion.behind: Keep this even-handed. The hunger for a king who conquers shows up on the right as a Christian strongman and on the left as a politics that will finally force the world right. Both want power that conquers rather than power that dies. Do not let the room aim it at one side.

discussion.q: Bell confesses the gauge of his hope on election night has told the truth about which kingdom he was serving. What did your last election night reveal about where your hope actually went?
discussion.behind: The wilderness temptation in a voting booth offers the kingdoms for one act of misdirected worship, the worship that says power saves. You are after honesty about where hope traveled when the returns came in, not which way anyone voted. Go first if needed.

objections.objection: A kingdom not of this world is just an excuse to retreat from politics and leave the vulnerable to whoever does not retreat. The prophets confronted kings. We should too.
objections.response: Bell grants this almost entirely. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people power crushes, and a faith with nothing to say to Pharaoh is not the faith of the Exodus. The warning is not against engagement. It is against the belief that engagement means seizing the throne. You can press hard against injustice and still refuse to believe Christ needs Caesar's sword to finish his work.

objections.objection: If our side simply wins, righteousness advances and the country is saved. Voting the right way is the most important thing a faithful Christian can do.
objections.response: This is the temptation Bell names in himself, the wilderness offer in a voting booth, the belief that the kingdom is one majority away. Answer it gently with the cross. The kingdom of God arrived through political defeat, through the state's machinery turned against the Son of God and failing to keep him buried. A faith that needs to win has confessed it no longer believes its own gospel can accomplish anything. Caring about an election is not the sin. Putting your hope there is.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you could change one thing about the world by simply winning an election, what would it be, and would winning actually fix it?
sessions.practice: This week, when you feel the pull to believe a political victory would finally fix things, pray one sentence instead, your kingdom come, your will be done, and notice how it reorders where your hope is sitting.
sessions.closingPrayer: Jesus, you stood in a high place and refused the kingdoms of the world, and you stood before Pilate and would not let your servants fight, and you took your throne by dying. We keep saying yes to the offer you refused and calling our yes obedience. Teach us the patience of a kingdom that does not need our majorities to arrive. Put our hope where it belongs, in the King who won by losing and cannot be voted out. Amen.
reflection: Where did my hope actually go the last time the returns came in, and what does that reveal about which kingdom I serve?
Do I believe the gospel can accomplish anything without political victory, or have I quietly decided it needs Caesar's sword?
What is the difference, in my own life, between being salt and attempting a coup, and which one have I been practicing?
sessions.teaching: Before Jesus preached a sermon or healed a single body, he was taken to a high place and shown every kingdom of the world by one who actually had them to give. All these I will give you, the tempter said, if you will fall down and worship me. This was not a hollow offer. The kingdoms were really on the table, and the price was a single act of worship aimed in the wrong direction. Jesus refused, and the refusal is the founding decision of his entire ministry. He would not take the kingdoms of the world on the terms by which the kingdoms of the world are taken. We reopen this every election cycle as though he never settled it. We ask how the church should hold power, how it should bend the levers of the state toward righteousness. These are not foolish questions. But they are downstream of a prior question the wilderness already answered, and we keep skipping the answer because we do not like it. The prior question is whether the kingdom of God advances by the means the world uses. Jesus said no in the desert, said it again to Pilate, and said it loudest on a cross. Give the strongest objection a full hearing, because it is not the objection of cowards. The prophets confronted kings. John the Baptist lost his head telling Herod the truth. Wilberforce used political power to end a slave trade. Bonhoeffer joined a plot against Hitler. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people that power crushes, and a faith with nothing to say to Pharaoh is not the faith of the Exodus. Grant the whole of it, because the half-grant is a cheat. The error is not engagement. The error is the belief that engagement means seizing the throne, that the kingdom is the kind you install by winning, that Christ needs to govern through Caesar because he cannot govern otherwise. Wilberforce did not try to make Britain the kingdom of God. He pressed a particular evil with the tools at hand and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. The difference between that and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup. Carry the governing text to its end. To Pilate, the only man in the room with the power to kill him, Jesus said his kingdom is not of this world, and if it were, his servants would be fighting. The proof he offers is the absence of fighting. A kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by definition. The crowd on Palm Sunday wanted exactly the king the tempter offered, one who would ride in and throw out Rome by force. They shouted hosanna, which means save us, and they meant save us from the empire. He rode in on a donkey, the animal of peace, and within the week the same crowd screamed for his blood, because he would not be that king. They wanted power that conquers. He gave them power that dies. And here I have to indict myself, because I have wanted the shortcut. I have stood in election seasons and felt the pull to believe that if my side simply won, the kingdom would advance, that righteousness was one majority away. That is the wilderness temptation in a voting booth. The gauge of my hope on election night has told me the truth about which kingdom I was actually serving, and the truth has not always flattered me. The cross does the decisive work. On the cross Jesus took the throne by the one means no empire understands. He did not seize power. He absorbed it. He let temple and empire do their worst and forgave them from inside the execution, and on the third day God overturned their verdict. That is how the kingdom comes. The church that grasps for political power has not understood the cross. It is trying to win a war that was already won by losing.

scriptureStudy.note: The devil takes Jesus to a very high mountain and shows him all the kingdoms and their glory. The vantage is the point. Power always looks like the answer from high enough up.

All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me. The kingdoms are real and the price is a single bow. The transaction is never honest about how small the bow feels and how total the surrender is.

Be gone, Satan, for it is written, you shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve. Jesus answers an offer of power with the first commandment. The issue under the kingdoms was always worship.
My kingdom is not of this world. The proof offered is that his servants are not fighting. A kingdom recognized by its refusal of the sword is a different kind of kingdom at the root.

Behold, your king comes to you, humble and mounted on a donkey. The Palm Sunday king was prophesied as the animal of peace, not the warhorse of conquest. The crowd missed the species and so missed the kingdom.

He humbled himself to the point of death on a cross, therefore God highly exalted him. The exaltation comes through the descent. The throne is taken by dying, which is the one method no empire can copy.

sessions.goingDeeper: Set the wilderness and Pilate scenes inside the larger New Testament theology of the powers. Read Colossians 2:15, where Christ disarms the rulers and authorities and triumphs over them in the cross, and ask how a triumph achieved by being executed reframes every theology of conquest. The advanced group should engage the Anabaptist and Hauerwasian reading, that the church is itself a polity and its first political act is to be the church, and then test it against the magisterial Reformation's two-kingdoms doctrine and against the genuine goods accomplished by Wilberforce and the abolitionists. The essay deliberately refuses both withdrawal and fusion, and a careful group should locate exactly where that middle stands and whether it is stable. Press the Christus Victor and substitutionary frames together. On the cross Christ both absorbs the verdict of the powers and pays a debt, and the political reading must not swallow the atonement whole or it becomes mere example. Then take up the hardest historical objection. Constantine's conversion and the Christianization of the empire arguably preserved the faith through centuries and built hospitals and schools, so was the Constantinian shift simply a fall, or a mixed providence that also corrupted. Bell's line is that the church traded a little theology for a little power until the cross became a flagpole, but a seminary group should weigh whether every alliance with power is that trade or whether faithfulness can survive proximity to a throne it does not worship.
sessions.caseStudy: It is the week after a national election, and your group meets on edge. A man who volunteered for the losing campaign says, with real grief, that he is afraid for the country and that he prayed for months that his side would win because he genuinely believed it was what God wanted. He is sincere, and he could be from either party, because this scenario plays out in both directions every cycle. The room is tempted to comfort him by agreeing the right side lost. Resist that. The pastoral question is not which side he was on. It is where his hope went, and what the depth of his fear reveals about where it had been resting. Honor his grief, because caring about the country is not the sin. Then ask gently whether a hope that can be shattered by a Tuesday in November was ever resting fully on the King who cannot be voted out. The wilderness offer comes in a voting booth to the left and the right alike, the belief that the kingdom is one majority away. Let him sit with where his hope actually traveled when the returns came in.

memoryVerse.text: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.

devotional.title: The Real Offer
devotional.body: The temptation in the wilderness was not a fake. The kingdoms were really on the table, shown from a high place by one who had the authority to give them, and the price was a single act of misdirected worship. We sometimes soften this story into a morality tale, but its danger is that the offer was genuine. Real power was available to Jesus on the spot, with no campaign and no war, for one bow. That is exactly how the temptation comes to the church. The kingdoms are real, the access is real, the seat at the table is real, and the price always seems modest, a small reorientation, a single bow toward power as the thing that saves. The tempter never announces the transaction. He shows the kingdoms and names a price that feels reasonable. Today, be honest about the offers in front of you. Where is real power or influence available to you, and what small bow is quietly attached. The bow is never labeled as worship. It is labeled as wisdom, as effectiveness, as just doing what works. Watch for the modest-seeming price, because that is where the whole soul changes hands.
devotional.prayer: Lord, the offers are real and the price feels small, and that is the trap. Give me eyes to see the bow hidden inside the bargain. Let me refuse the kingdoms that cost my worship.

devotional.title: Salt or a Coup
devotional.body: The difference between Wilberforce and Christian nationalism, Bell says, is the difference between salt and a coup. Jesus called his people the salt of the earth, and salt works by being scattered through a thing, preserving and seasoning from within, not by seizing the kitchen. Wilberforce pressed a particular evil with the tools at hand and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. He did not try to make Britain the kingdom of God. He was salt. The coup is different. The coup believes the kingdom must be installed by winning, that Christ cannot govern unless his people govern first. Today's question is not whether to engage. A faith with nothing to say to injustice has surrendered something it had no right to surrender. The question is how. Are you scattered through your sphere as salt, pressing for good while trusting God with the outcome, or are you trying to seize the kitchen, staking the kingdom itself on whether your side controls the room. Salt does its work and does not need to win to be faithful. Ask God which one you have been practicing, and whether your engagement still rests on his reign or on your victory.
devotional.prayer: Lord, make me salt and not a conqueror. Let me press for good with the tools at hand and trust you with the outcome. Free me from needing to win in order to be faithful.

devotional.title: The Absence of Fighting
devotional.body: To Pilate, Jesus offered a strange proof that his kingdom is not of this world. If it were, he said, my servants would be fighting. The evidence for the kingdom of God is the absence of the sword that every earthly kingdom requires. This disqualifies more of our political imagination than we want to admit. A kingdom that fights to install its king is, by Jesus' own test, a kingdom of this world no matter whose name is on the banner. The kingdom of God is recognizable precisely by its refusal to take up the means of conquest. Sit with how far this reaches. It is not only about literal violence. It is about the whole posture of grasping, of believing the cause of Christ depends on our seizing control. Every time we are sure the kingdom advances only if we win, we have confessed a kingdom of this world. Today, examine where your faith has quietly taken up the sword, where you have decided that the gospel needs you to seize something to make it safe. Then lay it down. The King you serve proved his kingdom by not letting his servants fight. Your refusal to grasp is not weakness. It is the mark of which kingdom you actually belong to.
