devotional.prayer: Jesus, you proved your kingdom by laying down the sword, and I keep reaching for it in your name. Show me where I have taken up what you refused. Teach me the strength of not grasping.

devotional.title: The King They Did Not Want
devotional.body: The Palm Sunday crowd wanted a king who would throw out Rome by force. The prophet had promised a king coming humble and mounted on a donkey, the animal of peace, and they cheered for a warhorse they were sure they saw. They shouted save us and meant save us from the empire. By week's end the same crowd wanted his blood, because he would not be the king they demanded. We are not so different. We still want the king who conquers rather than the one who dies, and the hunger runs in every direction. On the right it dreams of a strongman who will finally take the country back. On the left it dreams of a politics that will finally force the world right. Both want power that conquers. Both miss the donkey. Today, ask honestly which king you have been cheering for. When you imagine the world set right, do you picture a victory that crushes the other side, or a kingdom that comes the way Jesus came, low and refusing the sword. The crowd's disappointment became murderous because the real king would not perform the conquest they craved. Make sure your hosanna is aimed at the King who actually came, not the one you wish had.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have cheered for the king who conquers and turned away from the one who dies. Forgive the warhorse in my imagination. Teach me to want the King who came on a donkey and saved by losing.

devotional.title: Won by Losing
devotional.body: On the cross Jesus took the throne by the one means no empire understands. He did not seize power. He absorbed it. He let the combined authority of temple and empire do its worst, forgave them from inside the execution, and on the third day God overturned their verdict. Paul says he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them in the cross. Read that again. The triumph happened in the execution. The powers thought they were winning and were being disarmed in the very act. This is the pattern the church keeps forgetting. We are forever trying to win the war that was already won by losing, grasping for a power Christ refused because we do not trust the victory he already secured. A faith that needs to win has quietly confessed it no longer believes its own gospel can accomplish anything without Caesar's sword. End the week here. Where did your hope actually go the last time the returns came in. If a Tuesday in November can shatter it, it was not resting on the King who won by dying and cannot be voted out. Put your hope back where it belongs, in a kingdom that does not need your majorities to arrive, only your faithfulness while it comes.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, you triumphed in the place that looked like defeat, and I keep trying to win the war you already finished. Put my hope where it belongs, in a kingdom that needs no majority. Hold me faithful while it comes. Amen.

sessions.title: How the Religious Right Was Built
sessions.aim: To see that the political movement that taught a generation to read faithfulness as voting was assembled by named people in countable years, and can therefore be examined and repented.
sessions.summary: A young pastor who shadowed Bell assumed the religious right had always existed, that faithfulness had always come with a voter guide attached. Bell had to tell him the movement he took for the weather was younger than Bell's parents, built on purpose by people whose names we know in years we can count. It is not the ancient form of Christian political engagement but a specific coalition constructed in the 1970s around specific grievances. Bell grants the strongest defense first. Christians were not wrong to enter politics, the unborn are owed protection, a faith with no public voice has surrendered something. But the honest history complicates the founding story. The popular account says the movement rose in response to Roe in 1973. Randall Balmer argues, as one influential and contested reading, that in the years right after Roe white evangelical leaders were notably quiet about abortion, and that the fire that organized the movement was lit over the defense of segregated religious schools against federal interference. Bell is careful to say this is a contested thesis, not a closed verdict, and that the cleanest segregation-not-abortion story is too tidy for the evidence. What is fair to say is narrower and still uncomfortable. Race was woven into the movement's origins far more deeply than its founding myth admits. A thing built by men in years we can count can also, by grace, be examined and rebuilt.

keyScripture.why: The same wilderness offer of the kingdoms for a single bow names the bargain the religious right was offered, real access for a redirected worship.

discussion.q: The young pastor thought the religious right was the weather, the climate faith had always lived in. Why does a movement want you to believe it is eternal rather than built?
discussion.behind: A thing that hides the date it was built does not want you to know it could have been built differently. The aim is to loosen the assumption that the current fusion of faith and party is simply what serious Christians have always been.

discussion.q: Bell grants real weight to the movement's defense, that the unborn are owed protection and a faith with no public voice surrenders something. How do we hold those true things while still examining the movement?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. The point is not to abandon convictions about justice or the unborn. It is to hold them as Christians rather than as soldiers. Make sure pro-life participants feel honored, not dismissed, before the harder history lands.

discussion.q: Balmer argues, in a contested reading, that the fire was lit over segregated schools, not abortion, and Bell is careful to call it contested. Why does Bell refuse to give you the clean story?
discussion.behind: The cleanest segregation-not-abortion story is too tidy for the evidence. Race and abortion were braided, not sequential. The honest finding is narrower and still uncomfortable. Model for the room how to hold a hard claim without overstating it, and do not let anyone weaponize it into a simple verdict.

discussion.q: In 1980 the coalition chose Reagan, a divorced actor not notably devout, over Carter, a born-again Sunday school teacher. What did that choice reveal about the movement?
discussion.behind: It was not about personal piety. It was about political power, and it would prefer the powerful sinner to the pious opponent. This is the bow in the wilderness made visible. Notice that the same preference can run in any direction when a tribe wants power more than righteousness.

discussion.q: Bell says the movement made him before he could examine it, that he voted his way into what he thought was discipleship for years. Where have you carried a construction and called it the ancient faith?
discussion.behind: The closing self-implication of the whole study. We were all handed a hundred-year-old construction and called it the gospel. Nobody lied on purpose. They handed us what they were handed. Invite gentle, non-defensive recognition, and go first.

objections.objection: This is just an attack on pro-life Christians, dragging up race to shame people who only ever wanted to protect the unborn.
objections.response: Bell explicitly refuses this. He grants the unborn are owed protection and says knowing this history does not require anyone to abandon their convictions about justice or the unborn. The call is to hold those convictions as Christians rather than as soldiers. The history is uncomfortable, but Bell states the segregation thesis as contested, not settled, and the honest point is only that race was woven in more deeply than the founding myth admits. That is not an attack on the pro-life cause. It is honesty about a genealogy.

objections.objection: Fine, the religious right was built, so the answer is for Christians to just get out of politics entirely and stop imposing their faith on everyone.
objections.response: This is the opposite overcorrection, and Bell rules it out too. The error is not engagement. A faith with no public voice has surrendered something it had no right to surrender. The point is not withdrawal but refusing the bow that comes with the kingdoms, engaging as Christians who can still be corrected rather than as a tribe organized only to win. Examining the construction is not the same as abandoning the public square.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one thing you were taught about faith and politics growing up that you have never actually stopped to examine?
sessions.practice: This week, trace one political conviction you hold back to where you first received it. Ask whether you hold it as a Christian or as a soldier, and whether you could still be corrected on it. Write down what you find.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we were handed a building and told it was a revelation, and most of us never learned the date it went up. Forgive us for the bows we made without feeling the descent, for the times we wanted the kingdoms more than the cross. Give us the freedom to examine what we were handed without fear, to keep what is true, to repent of what was tribe dressed as faith, and to follow you rather than a coalition. Amen.
reflection: What political conviction have I held as a soldier rather than as a Christian, and could I still be corrected on it?
Where was I handed a construction and told it was the ancient faith, and have I ever stopped to learn the date it was built?
When have I preferred a powerful person who served my side over a faithful one who did not, and what did that preference reveal?
sessions.teaching: A young pastor who shadowed Bell for a summer assumed the religious right had always existed. He could not imagine a time when American Christians were not sorted into political camps, when faithfulness did not come with a voter guide attached. To him it was the weather, the climate faith had always lived in. Bell had to tell him the movement he took for the air itself was younger than Bell's parents, built on purpose by people whose names we know in years we can count. The thing that feels eternal was assembled inside living memory. That is the first thing to understand, and it is the thing most members of the movement do not know. The religious right is not the ancient form of Christian political engagement. It is a specific coalition, constructed in the 1970s, around specific grievances, by specific organizers. To say this is not to call it evil. Coalitions get built for good reasons too. It is to refuse the story the movement tells about itself, the story that it is simply what serious Christians have always been, the story that erases its own construction so it cannot be questioned. A thing that hides the date it was built does not want you to know it could have been built differently. Grant the strongest defense first, because it has truth in it. Christians were not wrong to enter politics. The unborn are owed protection. A faith with no public voice has surrendered something it had no right to surrender. Hold all of that. But the honest history complicates the founding story, and the complication is documented. The popular account says the movement rose spontaneously against Roe in 1973. Randall Balmer, who was inside evangelicalism, argues that this is largely a later rationalization, that in the years right after Roe white evangelical leaders were notably quiet about abortion, and that the fire which actually organized the movement was lit over the defense of segregated religious schools against federal interference. Be careful and fair here. This is a contested thesis, not a closed verdict. Other historians push back and date the real galvanizing more to Roe and the slow awakening of evangelicals to abortion. The cleanest segregation not abortion story is too tidy for the evidence. What is fair to say is narrower and still uncomfortable. Race was woven into the movement's origins far more deeply than its founding myth admits, whether or not it was the single spark. The pieces came together fast. Falwell founded the Moral Majority in 1979 and gathered conservative Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into one voting bloc. The 1980 election delivered the proof of concept when the coalition helped carry Reagan, a divorced Hollywood actor not notably devout, over Carter, a Southern Baptist Sunday school teacher who spoke openly of being born again. The choice told the truth. It was not about personal piety. It was about power, and it would prefer the powerful sinner to the pious opponent. Carry the governing text, because Scripture saw this exchange long before Falwell. In the wilderness the tempter offered all the kingdoms for one bow. The condition is always the same. The kingdoms are real and the price is a redirected worship. The religious right was offered real access and real influence, and the price was the slow reorientation of a faith around the winning of elections. Many bowed without ever feeling the descent. And I cannot tell this as an outsider, because the movement made me before I could examine it. The first Christianity I received out of atheism was already this fused thing, faith and party welded so tightly I assumed the weld was the gospel. Nobody lied to me on purpose. They handed me what they had been handed. I voted my way into what I thought was discipleship for years. Knowing this history does not require anyone to abandon their convictions about justice or the unborn. It requires holding them as Christians rather than as soldiers, refusing the bow that comes with the kingdoms, remembering we were handed a construction and not a revelation. Anything built by men in years we can count can also, by grace, be examined and rebuilt. We start by learning the date it went up.

scriptureStudy.note: Return to the wilderness offer one last time. All the kingdoms for one bow. The religious right was offered the same bargain in American form, real access for a redirected worship, and the price never announces itself.
Jesus answers with worship and service of God alone. The cure for the bargain is not better politics but a worship so settled it cannot be bought by access.
What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul. Ask it of a movement. What does it profit the church to gain a majority and forfeit the gospel that made it the church.
The Lord looks not on the outward appearance but on the heart. A coalition that preferred the powerful sinner to the pious opponent had already decided to look the way the Lord refuses to look.
Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns from the Lord. Trusting a coalition to save is the old sin of trusting in flesh, dressed for a new century.
We cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. A faith organized for winning will eventually be tempted against the truth, and Paul says that road is finally a dead end.

sessions.goingDeeper: Engage the historiography honestly rather than picking the version that flatters your side. Balmer's segregation thesis, advanced in his Politico essay and his longer work, rests substantially on the Bob Jones University tax-exemption fight and on Paul Weyrich's reported testimony about what finally mobilized evangelicals. Critics including historians sympathetic to neither hagiography nor caricature note that the Southern Baptist Convention's 1971 and post-Roe resolutions show a more mixed early posture on abortion, and that grassroots Catholic anti-abortion organizing predated and ran alongside the evangelical awakening, so the causation is braided rather than linear. A seminary group should practice holding a contested historical claim at exactly its evidentiary weight, neither dismissing the uncomfortable racial genealogy nor overstating it into a single tidy indictment. Bring in Daniel Williams's God's Own Party for the documented assembly history and Mark Noll's Scandal of the Evangelical Mind for the intellectual cost, the trade of theological labor for culture-war reflex. Then press the deeper theological question the history raises. If a movement was built around real moral concerns and also around grievance and racial defensiveness, how does the church repent of a genealogy without abandoning the genuine goods tangled inside it. The Reagan-over-Carter choice in 1980 is the cleanest case study. Work it slowly. What does it reveal that a coalition organized around Christian morality preferred the candidate whose life and faith fit its banner less but whose power served it more.
sessions.caseStudy: A lifelong Republican in your group, a man who has voted the straight ticket for forty years and led the pro-life ministry at your church, hears the segregation material and gets quiet, then firm. He says this feels like a setup, that the left has spent years trying to shame pro-life Christians by dragging up race, and that he resents a Bible study being used to make him apologize for caring about babies. His hurt is real and his pro-life conviction is honest. Here is the leader's task, and it is delicate. He is right that the phrase can be weaponized, and you should grant that fully and mean it. But the history is contested, not invented, and Bell states it as contested. The honest point is narrow. Race was woven into the movement's origins more deeply than its founding myth admits, and learning that does not require him to abandon a single conviction about the unborn. It asks him to hold that conviction as a Christian rather than a soldier. Do not let the room turn it into a verdict against him. Let him keep his cause and still examine its genealogy.

memoryVerse.text: For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?

devotional.title: The Weather and the Building
devotional.body: The young pastor thought the religious right was the weather, the climate faith had always lived in. Bell had to tell him it was a building, younger than his parents, assembled by named people in years we can count. This is the quiet danger of every inherited tradition. A thing that hides the date it was built does not want you to know it could have been built differently, because then you might examine it, and examination is the one thing a construction dressed as eternal cannot survive. Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for leaving the commandment of God and holding to the tradition of men, and the sting was that they could no longer tell the difference. They had received their traditions as if from heaven. We do the same. We absorb a political fusion in the air of a church and assume the fusion is the gospel, never asking when it was assembled or by whom. Today, take one conviction you hold about faith and public life and ask a simple question. Is this the commandment of God, or the tradition of men I received as if it were. You may keep it. But you should know which it is, and you cannot know until you ask.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I have held the traditions of men as if they came from you, and I cannot always tell them apart. Give me the honesty to ask which is which. Let me hold your commandment and examine the rest.

devotional.title: The Things That Are True
devotional.body: Before the hard history lands, hold the true things the movement was right about. The unborn are owed protection. Proverbs says to rescue those being taken away to death and to hold back those stumbling to the slaughter, and the one who says he did not know is not excused. A faith with no public voice has surrendered something it had no right to surrender. The defenders of the religious right are not fools, and to examine the movement is not to abandon the convictions that some who built it genuinely held. This matters, because the temptation when you learn a hard genealogy is to throw out everything tangled inside it, including the goods. Do not. The call is to hold your convictions about justice and the unborn as Christians rather than as soldiers, which means holding them more deeply, not less, but with open hands rather than a clenched fist. Today, name one public conviction you hold because you believe it honors God and your neighbor. Thank God for it. Then ask whether you have been holding it as a Christian, ready to be corrected and refusing to hate, or as a soldier, for whom the cause has swallowed the gospel that gave it.
devotional.prayer: Father, you call me to rescue the perishing and speak for the voiceless, and that call is good. Let me hold my convictions as a Christian and not a soldier, deeply and with open hands.

devotional.title: The Founding Myth
devotional.body: The popular story says the movement rose to defend the unborn, and the honest history says race and the defense of segregated institutions were woven in more deeply than the founding myth admits. This is contested, not a tidy verdict, and we hold it at exactly its weight. But Paul says to take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness and instead to expose them, and a movement, like a person, cannot repent of what it refuses to see. The instinct to protect the founding myth is strong, because the myth is cleaner than the genealogy and lets us feel pure. But a story too clean to be true does not protect us. It only delays the reckoning. Today, practice the harder honesty on something close to home. Is there a story you tell about your own family, your church, your nation, or yourself that is cleaner than the evidence, edited to remove the uncomfortable part. You do not have to broadcast it. But bring it into the light before God, who already knows the unedited version and loves you inside it. Exposing the darkness is not betrayal. It is the only path to a repentance that actually heals, rather than a peace that only pretends.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I edit my stories cleaner than the truth and call the edit peace. Expose what I have hidden, in my history and my heart. Let me face the unedited version in your light and your mercy.

devotional.title: The Powerful Sinner
devotional.body: In 1980 the coalition chose Reagan, a divorced actor not notably devout, over Carter, a born-again Sunday school teacher. The choice told the truth about the movement. It was not about personal piety. It was about power, and it would prefer the powerful sinner who served the cause to the pious opponent who did not. The Lord told Samuel he does not look on the outward appearance but on the heart, that man sees what his own eyes prefer to see. A tribe that wants power more than righteousness will always end up preferring the candidate who delivers, whatever his life, and will learn to call the preference wisdom. And note carefully, this temptation has no party. Any side, when it wants power badly enough, will choose the useful sinner over the inconvenient saint. Today, examine your own preferences. When have you excused in a leader who served your side what you would have condemned in one who did not. That double standard is the tell. It reveals that somewhere the cause replaced the Christ, that you began looking the way the Lord refuses to look, on the outward usefulness rather than the heart. Ask God to give you a single standard, applied to your own side first.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you look on the heart while I look at who serves my side. Forgive my double standard, harsh on the other and soft on my own. Give me one measure, and start it with me.

devotional.title: Handed a Construction
devotional.body: Bell ends inside the indictment. The movement made him before he could examine it. The first Christianity he received out of atheism was already fused, faith and party welded so tightly he assumed the weld was the gospel, and he voted his way into what he thought was discipleship for years. Nobody lied to him. They handed him what they had been handed. Paul reminds Timothy of the sincere faith that lived first in his grandmother and his mother and now in him, a good inheritance passed down through real love. Inheritances can carry treasure and rubble in the same box. The faith handed to you came through people who loved you and also carried constructions they never examined, and the work of a lifetime is to keep the treasure and set down the rubble without despising the hands that passed you both. End the week with gratitude and honesty together. Thank God for the people who handed you faith, even imperfectly. Then ask for the freedom to examine what you were handed without fear, to keep what is true, to repent of what was tribe dressed as faith, and to follow Christ rather than a coalition. Anything built by people in years you can count can also, by grace, be examined and rebuilt.
devotional.prayer: Father, thank you for the people who handed me faith, who loved me and also passed me things they never examined. Give me freedom to keep the treasure and set down the rubble. Let me follow Christ and not a coalition. Amen.

leaderPrimer: You did not have to do this, and the fact that you said yes matters more than you know. So before you open the first session, sit with me for a while. This study will only go as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the material. It is settling your own heart. The aim of this series is narrow and it is hard. It is to recover what the phrase Christian nationalism actually names, to draw a clean line between loving a country and worshiping it, and to keep the cross over the flag in a room full of people who arrived with that order already scrambled in different directions. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to win an argument. It is not to move people to the left or the right. It is not to produce a room that finally agrees with you. If anyone leaves the series voting differently but loving Christ no more than before, the study failed, no matter how satisfying the conversion felt. Keep that in front of you, because the single greatest danger you face as a leader is the temptation to turn this into a political brawl, and that temptation will not announce itself as a brawl. It will arrive dressed as truth-telling, as finally saying the thing that needs saying, as the righteous heat of being right. Refuse it. The moment the room splits into a side that is winning and a side that is losing, the study has stopped doing its work, because its work was to indict every tribe, including yours and including mine. So here is how you refuse the brawl in practice. Go first into every hard place. Before you ask anyone else to confess where their love of country runs out of order, confess yours out loud, specifically, without softening it into a humble-sounding non-confession. When the segregation history in session five lands hard, model holding it as contested rather than weaponizing it. When the flags-in-the-sanctuary session tempts the progressives in the room to feel superior, turn the knife toward them too, because pride strips a platform as easily as idolatry drapes one. Even-handedness is not a tone you adopt. It is a discipline you practice in real time, catching the right in one session and the left in the next, and refusing to let the room aim the indictment safely at the people who are not present. Now keep the room safe, because depth requires safety and these are not safe topics. Safety here does not mean comfort. It means that a person can be wrong out loud without being humiliated, can change his mind without losing face, can say the half-formed honest thing without it being used against him next week. Set that expectation in the first session and guard it every session after. The facilitator script gives you words for this. Use them. The ground rules are not throat-clearing. They are the walls that make honesty possible. You will face three rooms, and you should know them before they arrive. The first is the angry person, the one who came certain this study is an attack on people like him. Do not match his heat and do not rush to disarm him. Find the half of his anger that is true, because there usually is one, and say it back to him better than he said it, so he knows he was heard before he is answered. The man who feared the phrase was right that it gets thrown carelessly. Grant that fully and mean it, and you will find the anger has somewhere to go besides escalation. The second is the hurt person, the one whose father served, whose grief is real, who hears the dates 1954 and 1956 as an insult to someone he loved. Do not argue with grief. Honor the person and the love, and let the hard fact stand beside the honor without canceling it. You are not there to win against his pain. You are there to show him that the truth and his father can both stand in the same room. The third is the silent room, the one where nobody will go first because everyone is calculating the cost. The silent room is almost always a fear room, and the cure is not a better question. It is your own vulnerability. Go first, confess first, be unsure first, and the room will slowly follow you into the honesty you modeled. Silence after a hard question is usually people thinking, not people refusing. Count to ten in your head before you rescue it. Now the part that matters most, the part it would be easiest to skip. Your own heart. You cannot lead people somewhere you have not gone. If you walk into this study as the one who already sees clearly, the wise guide helping the confused congregation find its way out of idolatry, you have already failed, because the writer of these essays does not stand there and neither can you. Bell came up out of atheism into a faith already fused with the flag. He still has flags on his own platform he has not moved. He writes from inside the indictment, and the power of the whole series depends on you doing the same. So before session one, do the work yourself. Find the place where your love of country runs out of order. Name the election night when your hope went somewhere it should not have. Locate the conviction you hold as a soldier rather than as a Christian. If you cannot find any of these in yourself, you are not ready to lead, because either you are without sin in this matter, which the gospel says you are not, or you cannot yet see your own, which means you will lead from above the room instead of inside it. The leader who has repented can call others to repentance without contempt. The leader who has not will turn the study into a weapon, however gently he holds it. Here is your charge. You are not the judge of this room. You are a fellow defendant who happens to be holding the readings. Lead like one. Let the weight of these sessions rest on you first and hardest. Refuse every chance to make this about the people who are not present. Keep the cross above the flag in your own heart before you ask anyone else to, and when you fail at it, say so out loud, because your failure honestly named will teach the room more than your competence ever could. The goal is not a room that agrees with you at the end. The goal is a room full of people, you first, who can love their country with a love that can still tell it the truth, and who can no longer remember why they ever thought the flag belonged over the cross. Go gently. Go honestly. Go first.

faq.q: Is this study just a way to attack conservatives who love their country?
faq.a: No, and the study works hard to prove it. The first essay grants at length that loving your country is not a sin, that Scripture told exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon, and that the people who throw the phrase carelessly are committing their own sin. The target is never patriotism. It is the fusion that cannot repent, the love that has grown too large to be corrected. A conservative who loves his country, honors its soldiers, and still keeps Christ above it has nothing to fear here. The line the study draws runs through every heart, not down one party's platform. And the study indicts the left as plainly as the right, asking the progressive whether he trusts the state to save and fears religion in public only when it is the wrong religion. If it were an attack on one tribe, it would not keep turning the knife toward the other.

faq.q: Is this just a way for the left to baptize its own politics as the real gospel?
faq.a: It would be, if it spared the left, and it does not. The study presses the progressive as hard as the conservative. It names the trust in government to deliver salvation as the same trade Israel made when they wanted a king to be like the nations. It warns that removing a flag can be a sneer of performed sophistication as easily as keeping it can be idolatry. It catches the hunger for a politics that will finally force the world right as the same conquest theology it condemns on the right, just wearing a different color. The gospel here is not a party's program with a cross stapled on. It is the refusal of every tribe's claim to be the kingdom. If your politics survives this study completely unscathed, you were not reading carefully.

faq.q: What is the actual difference between patriotism and Christian nationalism?
faq.a: Patriotism is love and settled care for a particular place and its people, and it can be criticized, corrected, and repented, because it does not claim ultimate loyalty. Christian nationalism, in the careful sense the scholars Whitehead and Perry gave it, is a cultural framework that fuses national and Christian identity into one, holds the nation has a covenant with God, and believes the kingdom of Christ can be advanced by capturing the state. The word that matters is fuses. The test is what happens when your country and your Christ command different things. The patriot grieves and obeys Christ. The nationalist has arranged his theology so the conflict can never arise. Love can be corrected. Worship cannot. That single difference is the whole line.

faq.q: Are the founders not proof that America was founded as a Christian nation?
faq.a: The historical record is more mixed than the founding myth allows. The historian Mark Noll has shown that the colonists did not arrive with a unified Christian nation in mind and that the founders ranged from devout Calvinists to skeptical deists, and the Constitution names no God and establishes no church on purpose. The phrases many treat as ancient proof are recent. One nation under God entered the Pledge in 1954 and in God we trust became the national motto in 1956, both under the pressure of the Cold War. None of this means faith had no role in the founding. It means the clean story of a Christian founding lost and waiting to be reclaimed is itself a later construction, and a covenant you can date to an act of Congress is a national mood that learned to talk like one.

faq.q: Is the study saying Christians should withdraw from politics entirely?
faq.a: No, and it rules that out as firmly as it rules out fusion. The fourth essay grants the whole of the case for engagement. The prophets confronted kings. Wilberforce ended a slave trade. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people power crushes. The error the study names is not engagement but the belief that engagement means seizing the throne, that the kingdom must be installed by winning. The difference between Wilberforce and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup. You can press hard against injustice with the tools at hand and still refuse to believe Christ needs Caesar's sword to finish his work. Withdrawal and fusion are both errors. The study walks the harder line between them.

faq.q: If there is no neutral public square, is not driving faith out just another establishment?
faq.a: Yes, and the study agrees, drawing on Lesslie Newbigin, who saw exactly this. There is no neutral public square. The question is never whether faith shapes public life but which faith and how. A secularism that imagines itself neutral is a different establishment wearing the mask of neutrality, and the believer who resents being told only his convictions must be left at the door is not wrong to resent it. But this is a critique of false neutrality, not a defense of fusion. The answer to a hidden establishment is not to enthrone our own. It is honest, humble public faith that can still be corrected, that brings its convictions into the square openly while refusing to make the nation its god.

faq.q: Why bring up race when talking about the religious right? Is that not just shaming pro-life Christians?
faq.a: The study is careful here on purpose. It states the segregation thesis, associated with Randall Balmer, as contested and not as a settled verdict, and it explicitly refuses to use it to shame anyone. It grants that the unborn are owed protection and that knowing this history requires no one to abandon a single conviction about justice or the unborn. The honest point is narrow and still uncomfortable. Race and the defense of segregated institutions were woven into the movement's origins more deeply than its founding myth admits, whether or not they were the single spark. That is honesty about a genealogy, not an attack on a cause. A movement, like a person, can examine its own history without being destroyed by it, and a cause held as a Christian rather than a soldier can survive learning the truth about where it came from.

faq.q: Does a kingdom not of this world mean Jesus did not care about justice here and now?
faq.a: No. When Jesus told Pilate his kingdom is not of this world, the proof he offered was the absence of fighting, his servants not taking up the sword. He was not saying his kingdom has no bearing on this world. He was saying it does not come from this world's source and does not advance by this world's method. The same Jesus announced good news to the poor and release to the captives and confronted the powers of his day with the truth. The kingdom he brings reorders this world precisely by refusing to install itself through conquest. Caring about justice is not the error. Believing justice arrives only when our side seizes the throne is the error, because the cross shows the kingdom coming through what looked like defeat.

faq.q: Is it really wrong to have a flag in the church sanctuary?
faq.a: The study deliberately refuses to make this a rule about the cloth. It grants that a flag can express genuine gratitude, can honor members who served and died, and that removing it can be a sneer of performed pride as easily as keeping it can be idolatry. The object is not the disease. The question the study asks is about geography and meaning. Where does it stand, lobby or platform, and what is it permitted to mean. A symbol placed in the jealous space beside the Word and the table will, over time, be read as the cross's equal, and children absorb that equality before they can name it. The point is not to hand you a verdict on your church's furniture. It is to make you read the room you worship in as a sermon and ask honestly what it has been teaching.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the leader and the writer instead of the real offenders?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is the message. Bell came up out of atheism into a faith already fused with the flag, and he still has flags on his own platform he has not moved. He writes from inside the indictment, not from a safe distance, and the study asks every leader to do the same. The reason is not false modesty. It is that you cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue, and you cannot call others to repentance from a height without turning the call into contempt. A study that pointed only at the absent offenders would let everyone present off the hook and change no one. By keeping the leader and the writer inside the indictment, the study makes repentance possible for the people actually in the room, which is the only place change ever happens.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not all of this just religion arguing about how to grab power either way?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study earns the right to answer it by criticizing exactly the power-grabbing you are wary of. The whole series argues that the faith of Jesus refuses to advance by seizing the state, that Jesus turned down the kingdoms of the world when they were genuinely offered, and that a Christianity which needs political victory has confessed it no longer believes its own gospel. If you have seen religion used as a tool for power, the study agrees that is a corruption and names it as one, on the right and the left both. What it offers instead is a faith whose founder took a throne by being executed and forgiving his executioners, which is the opposite of a power grab. You do not have to accept the faith to notice the study is arguing against the very thing you distrust.

faq.q: If Christians do not try to make the laws Christian, will the country not just drift into immorality?
faq.a: The study does not counsel passivity, and it does not promise that refusing fusion makes a country righteous. It says you can labor hard for justice and the good of your neighbor while refusing to make the nation your god, that these are not in tension. The deeper answer is that a faith which can only hold a country by capturing its laws has a thin view of how God actually works. The early church changed the world it lived in without controlling a single law, by being a different kind of community, telling the truth, welcoming the stranger, refusing to win by the means that required it to stop being the church. Laws matter and Christians may work for good ones. But a country is not saved by its statutes, and a church that believes it is has put its hope where the gospel never put it.

faq.q: Does refusing Christian nationalism mean I have to vote a certain way?
faq.a: No, and a study that delivered a voting instruction would betray its own argument. The series indicts the right and the left both and refuses to baptize either party as the kingdom. Its concern is not which lever you pull but where your hope rests when the returns come in. Two believers who have genuinely refused the fusion can still vote differently in good conscience, weighing competing goods and arriving at different judgments, because political wisdom is not the same as ultimate loyalty. The study asks you to hold your political convictions as a Christian rather than a soldier, ready to be corrected, refusing to hate the people across the aisle, and never putting in an election the hope that belongs to Christ. What you do with the ballot after that is between you and God.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I do not have a seminary degree or any training?
faq.a: You lead it the way it was built to be led, by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than argument. The new material adds teaching notes, scripture studies, and a leader primer precisely so you are not improvising. But the real qualification is not training. It is willingness to go first, to be honest about your own heart, to keep the room safe for people who disagree, and to refuse to turn the study into a brawl. A leader who has examined his own love of country and found it out of order can guide this faithfully with no degree at all. A leader with three degrees who stands above the room will do it harm. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart, and trust the material.

timeline.event: The Edict of Milan, issued under Constantine and Licinius, grants toleration to Christians across the Roman Empire and ends official persecution, beginning the long alignment of church and imperial power.
The Edict of Thessalonica under Theodosius makes Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire, completing the shift from a persecuted faith to an established one.
Augustine completes The City of God, written as Rome falls, arguing that no earthly nation is the city of God and that two cities built by two loves are mixed together in this age.

The Peace of Westphalia ends Europe's wars of religion and entrenches the modern nation-state, tying religious identity to the sovereign's territory under the principle that the ruler's religion is the land's.
The United States Constitution takes effect, naming no God and establishing no church, and the First Amendment follows in 1791, setting the new nation apart from the established churches of Europe.
Francis Bellamy writes the Pledge of Allegiance, notably without the words under God, which would not be added for another sixty-two years.
The Scopes trial in Dayton, Tennessee, hands fundamentalism a cultural defeat that drives its conviction of a besieged Christian civilization underground, where it hardens.
Congress inserts the phrase one nation under God into the Pledge of Allegiance at the height of the Cold War, to mark the difference between a godly America and a godless Soviet enemy.
In God we trust becomes the official national motto, displacing the older and more modest e pluribus unum.

Robert Bellah publishes Civil Religion in America, naming the shared rituals and beliefs through which the nation understands itself before the transcendent, an instrument that can humble a nation or flatter it.

The Southern Baptist Convention passes a resolution taking a notably moderate early position on abortion, evidence later cited that white evangelical leaders were not immediately mobilized by the issue.

The Supreme Court decides Roe v. Wade, the decision the religious right's founding story credits as the spark, though the historical record of the years just after is more mixed than the story allows.
Jerry Falwell founds the Moral Majority, gathering conservative Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into a single voting bloc around the sense that Christian America is under siege.
The coalition helps carry Ronald Reagan, a divorced actor not notably devout, over Jimmy Carter, a born-again Sunday school teacher, revealing the movement to be about power more than personal piety.

Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry publish Taking America Back for God, the careful sociological study that defines and measures Christian nationalism as a cultural framework fusing civic and Christian identity.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here. Before we start, three things. First, this study was written to indict every tribe, including mine and yours, so we are not here to score points against the people who are not in the room. Second, nobody has to perform certainty. You can be unsure out loud, and you can change your mind. Third, the writer puts himself inside everything he says, and so will we. We are not pointing from a safe distance. We are standing in it. Tonight we are looking at this theme together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the essay says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the week we are about to walk into, because none of this matters if it stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because Bell does not resolve it either and neither should we. Take the weight of this out with you rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go, and then I will see you next time. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation.

bibliography.title: Taking America Back for God: Christian Nationalism in the United States
bibliography.author: Andrew L. Whitehead and Samuel L. Perry
bibliography.note: The careful sociological study that defines Christian nationalism as a cultural framework fusing civic and Christian identity, and measures it across a spectrum. The empirical spine of session 1.

bibliography.title: The Irony of American History
bibliography.author: Reinhold Niebuhr
bibliography.note: Where Niebuhr names patriotism as a high devotion that becomes demonic when it claims the unconditioned loyalty belonging to God alone. Central to session 2.

bibliography.title: Civil Religion in America
bibliography.author: Robert N. Bellah
bibliography.note: The 1967 essay that names civil religion as a real religion with sacred objects and holy days, the lens for the flags-in-the-sanctuary session.

bibliography.title: America's God: From Jonathan Edwards to Abraham Lincoln
bibliography.author: Mark A. Noll
bibliography.note: Shows the colonists did not arrive with a unified Christian nation in mind and warns against reading providence directly off national events. Grounds the history in session 1.

bibliography.title: Fundamentalism and American Culture
bibliography.author: George M. Marsden
bibliography.note: Traces how fundamentalism came to see itself as the last defender of a Christian civilization under siege, hardening after the 1925 Scopes trial.

bibliography.title: Jesus and John Wayne: How White Evangelicals Corrupted a Faith and Fractured a Nation
bibliography.author: Kristin Kobes Du Mez
bibliography.note: Documents how a militant vision of Christian manhood fused with the defense of the nation across the twentieth century. Bell urges reading the footnotes even where readers distrust the conclusions.

bibliography.title: The Gospel in a Pluralist Society
bibliography.author: Lesslie Newbigin
bibliography.note: Argues there is no neutral public square and that a gospel which only blesses a culture loses its power to call that culture to repentance. Used on both sides of session 1's even-handedness.

bibliography.title: After Christendom
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas
bibliography.note: Insists the first task of the church is to be the church, not to run the country. Handle with care as one voice among several, not the study's settled position.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon
bibliography.note: Source of the claim that the church does not have a social strategy, the church is a social strategy. Anchors session 4. Use with care, as Bell affirms public engagement too.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine
bibliography.note: The two cities built by two loves, mixed in this age so no earthly nation is the city of God. The deep background for sessions 1, 2, and 4.

bibliography.title: The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind
bibliography.author: Mark A. Noll
bibliography.note: Source of the line that the scandal of the evangelical mind is that there is not much of one, naming the intellectual cost of trading theology for culture war. Anchors session 5.

bibliography.title: God's Own Party: The Making of the Christian Right
bibliography.author: Daniel K. Williams
bibliography.note: Traces how Falwell's Moral Majority gathered Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into a single voting bloc. The documented assembly history for session 5.

bibliography.title: The Real Origins of the Religious Right
bibliography.author: Randall Balmer
bibliography.note: The Politico essay arguing segregation, not abortion, lit the movement's fire. Bell presents it as one influential and contested reading, not a settled verdict. Leader to confirm before stating it as fact, and present it as contested.

The Myth of a Christian Nation, Gregory Boyd, a pastor's accessible case against fusing the kingdom of God with national power, a gentle next step after this study.

glossary.definition: A cultural framework that fuses national identity with a particular Christian identity, holds the nation has a covenant with God, and believes its laws should privilege that faith. It is the fusion that cannot be questioned, not ordinary love of country.
Love and settled care for a particular place and its people. Unlike nationalism, it can be criticized, corrected, and repented, because it does not claim ultimate loyalty.

The shared beliefs and rituals through which a nation understands itself in relation to the transcendent, such as appeals to God in inaugural addresses and the sacred status of founding documents. It can humble a nation or flatter it.

The long era and arrangement in which the church and the state were fused, and being a citizen and being a Christian were assumed to be the same thing. Much of the study asks what faith looks like after Christendom ends.
The pattern, named for the emperor Constantine, of the church aligning itself with state power and learning to advance its mission through the machinery of empire rather than through the cross.

The theological idea that God rules the world in two distinct ways, through the gospel and the church on one hand and through civil government on the other, so the two should not be collapsed into one.
Augustine's image of the earthly city built by love of self and the city of God built by love of God, mixed together in this age so that no nation is wholly either one.

The theological idea that God gives genuine gifts, such as order, beauty, and justice, to all people and societies, believing or not, which lets Christians honor good in their country without worshiping it.

The position that the civil law of a modern nation should be directly governed by the detailed laws of Old Testament Israel. It is one of the more extreme expressions of wanting the state to enforce a particular faith.

God's governing of history. Scripture is far more reticent than we are about reading providence directly off national events, so we cannot simply assume God favored this army or blessed that founding.
The capacity, drawn from the biblical prophets, to name a nation's sins and call it to repentance from inside, rather than only blessing it. A faith fused with the nation loses this capacity.

Augustine's definition of sin as love poured out in the wrong proportion, a lesser good loved as though it were the greatest. The nationalist does not love his country too much, he loves it out of order.
Treating something other than God as ultimate. The idol is rarely a bad thing, it is usually a good thing that has been asked to be God, which is exactly how a country becomes one.

The political organization founded by Jerry Falwell in 1979 that gathered conservative Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into a single voting bloc, a key piece of the assembly of the religious right.
